abstract: |
  Frontier AI laboratories must decide when to build irreversible compute capacity, how much, and how to split it between inference, which earns revenue now, and training, which pays off only if Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) arrives.
  I develop a real-options model with regime-switching demand, a duopoly entry game, and endogenous default.
  The optimal training fraction has a closed form that rises with the switch's arrival rate and does not depend on scale.
  At baseline a single firm that can choose its scale when the switch arrives waits for it, while in the duopoly one firm invests before the switch, because waiting leads to a post-switch race that competes away the rent from leading; the equilibrium is verified numerically, not shown unique.
  Operating costs create a shutdown boundary at which a firm stops operating without debt, and when it trains enough, optimism about the switch lowers it ("faith-based survival").
  A mistaken belief costs value mainly through the training allocation.
  For a single firm with precommitted post-switch scale, believing the arrival rate is 0.02 when it is 0.10 costs 32% of value, against 1.3% for an optimistic error of the same size and 13% for one of the same proportion.
  Errors matched in expected years to the switch cost about the same, and the latter optimist is eleven times as likely as an informed firm to reach its shutdown boundary within five years.
  A stylized calibration maps training allocations assigned to four AI lab archetypes into implied beliefs and their consequences.
keywords:
  - real options
  - irreversible capacity investment
  - artificial intelligence
  - duopoly entry timing
  - default risk
